DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
Timely Petition for Review under §19(b) having been filed by Respondent herein and 
notice given to all parties, the Commission, after considering the issues of causal connection, 
medical expenses, temporary total disability, and prospective medical care, and being advised of 
the facts and law, affirms and adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which is attached hereto and 
made a part hereof.  The Commission further remands this case to the Arbitrator for further 
proceedings for a determination of a further amount of temporary total compensation or of 
compensation for permanent disability, if any, pursuant to Thomas v. Industrial Commission, 78 
Ill.2d 327, 399 N.E.2d 1322, 35 Ill.Dec. 794 (1980). 
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed September 16, 2025, is hereby affirmed and adopted. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay to 
Petitioner interest under §19(n) of the Act, if any. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall have credit 
for all amounts paid, if any, to or on behalf of Petitioner on account of said accidental injury.

Arbitrator for further proceedings consistent with this Decision.

An Application for Adjustment of Claim was filed in this matter, and a Notice of Hearing was mailed to each 
party.  The matter was heard by the Honorable Jeanne L. AuBuchon, Arbitrator of the Commission, in the city 
of Mt. Vernon, Illinois, on August 19, 2025.  After reviewing all of the evidence presented, the Arbitrator 
hereby makes findings on the disputed issues checked below, and attaches those findings to this document. 
 
DISPUTED ISSUES 
 
A.

 Diseases Act? 
 
B. 
 Was there an employee-employer relationship? 
 
C.

FINDINGS 
 
On the date of accident, November 12, 2024, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions of 
the Act.   
 
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did exist between Petitioner and Respondent.   
 
On this date, Petitioner did sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment. 
 
Timely notice of this accident was given to Respondent. 
 
Petitioner's current condition of ill-being is causally related to the accident. 
 
In the year preceding the injury, Petitioner earned $78,950.00.; the average weekly wage was $1,518.27. 
 
On the date of accident, Petitioner was 42 years of age, married with 3 dependent children. 
 
Respondent has not paid all reasonable and necessary charges for all reasonable and necessary medical 
services.   
 
Respondent shall be given a credit of $0 for TTD, $0 for TPD, $0 for maintenance, and $0 for other benefits, for 
a total credit of $0. 
 
Respondent is entitled to a credit of $if any under Section 8(j) of the Act. 
 
ORDER 
 
Respondent shall pay the reasonable and necessary medical services outlined in Petitioner’s Exhibit 1, as 
provided in Sections 8(a) and 8.2 of the Act.   
 
Respondent shall be given a credit for medical benefits that have been paid, and Respondent shall hold 
Petitioner harmless from any claims by any providers of the services for which Respondent is receiving this 
credit, as provided in Section 8(j) of the Act.  
 
Respondent shall authorize and pay for the prospective treatment, specifically surgery and follow-up treatment  
recommended by Dr. Bradley.  
 
 
 
In no instance shall this award be a bar to subsequent hearing and determination of an additional amount of 
medical benefits or compensation for a temporary or permanent disability, if any.   
 
RULES REGARDING APPEALS  Unless a party files a Petition for Review within 30 days after receipt of this 
decision, and perfects a review in accordance with the Act and Rules, then this decision shall be entered as the 
decision of the Commission.   
 
STATEMENT OF INTEREST RATE  If the Commission reviews this award, interest at the rate set forth on the Notice 
of Decision of Arbitrator shall accrue from the date listed below to the day before the date of payment; 
however, if an employee's appeal results in either no change or a decrease in this award, interest shall not 
accrue.

PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 
This matter proceeded to trial on August 19, 2025, pursuant to Sections 19(b) and 8(a) of 
the Illinois Workers’ Compensation Act (hereinafter “the Act”).  The issues in dispute are: 1) the 
causal connection between the accident and the Petitioner’s left shoulder condition; 2) payment of 
medical bills; and 3) entitlement to prospective medical care. 
 
FINDINGS OF FACT 
 
At the time of the accident, the Petitioner was 42 years old and employed by the 
Respondent as a residential services supervisor.  (AX1, T. 9-10)  On November 12, 2024, she was 
assisting to place an aggressive individual in a humane wrap when he bucked out of it and kicked 
her in the left shoulder.  (T. 10-11)  She felt burning in her shoulder and could not put her arm 
behind her back.  (T. 11) 
The Petitioner acknowledged being treated for pain in her left shoulder in May 2024.  (T. 
12-13)  Records from Dr. JT Davis, an orthopedic surgeon at the Orthopaedic Institute of Southern 
Illinois (OISI), reflect that an MRI of the left shoulder performed on May 24, 2024, showed: 1) 
rotator cuff tendinosis, an insertional tear of the supraspinatus anteriorly involving greater than 50 
percent of the tendon thickness without definite full-thickness tear or tendon retraction and a less 
extensive partial-thickness tear more proximally: 2) a small amount of fluid in the 
subacromial/subdeltoid bursa; 3) degenerative change of the acromioclavicular (AC) joint and 
marrow edema and erosive change of the distal clavicle; and 4) capsular thickening/scarring that 
may have been related to old injury or chronic sequela of adhesive capsulitis, as well as 
intrasubstance degeneration and suspected anatomic variation of the glenoid labrum.  (RX5) 
On June 18, 2024, the Petitioner saw Dr. Davis’s physician assistant Jeremy Palmer for left 
shoulder pain that began in March without inciting injury.  (Id.)  PA Palmer diagnosed pain in the 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 2 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
left shoulder, traumatic incomplete tear of the left rotator cuff and strain of the right rotator cuff.  
(Id.)  He performed diagnostic and therapeutic steroid injections of both shoulders and gave home 
exercises.  (Id.)  The Petitioner testified that the injection helped but by September 2024 had worn 
off “just a little bit.”  (T. 14, 27)  She reported to PA Palmer on September 4, 2024, that she was 
getting some relief with the injection, but her shoulder was still painful.  (PX5)  PA Palmer stated 
that they discussed continued conservative care versus surgery.  (Id.)  The Petitioner wanted to 
schedule surgery for December.  (Id.)  She testified that at the time of the accident on November 
12, 2024, her shoulder “was feeling okay.”  (T. 14)  She denied alleging a work-related accident 
to avoid a copay for the surgery recommended by Dr. Davis.  (T. 29-30) 
Following the work accident on November 12, 2024, the Petitioner was sent to SIH 
Workcare, where she was diagnosed with an unspecified injury of the muscles and tendons of the 
rotator cuff and referred to OISI.  (T. 11-12, PX3) 
On November 27, 2024, the Petitioner saw PA Palmer and complained of immediate left 
shoulder pain following the incident at work.  (PX4, RX5)  An examination included positive tests 
regarding the biceps tendon (Yergason’s and Speed’s) and impingement (Neer and Hawkins).  (Id.)  
PA Palmer diagnosed traumatic complete tear of the left rotator cuff, tendinopathy of the left biceps 
tendon and impingement syndrome of the left shoulder.  (Id.)  He recommended arthroscopic 
rotator cuff repair, biceps tenodesis and subacromial decompression.  (Id.) 
The Petitioner testified that she sought a second opinion from Dr. Matthew Bradley, an 
orthopedic surgeon at Metro East Orthopedics, whom she saw on December 19, 2019.  (T. 16, 
PX5)  She described the previous medical care for her left shoulder and described the accident and 
gave Dr. Bradley the MRI scan from May 2024.  (PX5)  Dr. Bradley performed an examination 
with impingement (Neer/Jobs/Hawkins) and biceps tests (Speed’s/Yergurson’s) being noted as 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 3 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
positive and equivocal and a test for superior labrum anterior-posterior (SLAP) tear (O’Brien’s) 
being equivocal.  (Id.)  A cross-chest test was negative for AC joint pain.  (Id.)  He read the MRI 
as showing rotator cuff tendinosis and a tear of the supraspinatus involving greater than 50 percent.  
(Id.) 
Dr. Bradley diagnosed a rotator cuff tear and stated it was possible that the new injury had 
worsened the tear and possibly created a full-thickness tear.  (Id.)  He recommended a repeat MRI 
to evaluate the rotator cuff and look at the labrum and biceps tendon.  (Id.)  He opined that the 
work injury caused significant worsening of the Petitioner’s pain and loss of function of her left 
shoulder and, therefore, was causally related to the increased symptoms and need for further work 
up and evaluation.  (Id.) 
The MRI arthrogram was performed on December 19, 2024, at MRI Partners of 
Chesterfield.  (PX6)  Radiologist Dr. James Schoen noted: 1) insertional supraspinatus tendinitis 
and subinsertional enthesopathic change but no high-grade partial-thickness or full-thickness 
rotator cuff tear; 2) nondisplaced SAP) tear with otherwise normal glenohumeral articulation and 
intact long head biceps; and 3) mild AC joint arthropathy.  (Id.) 
The Petitioner returned to Dr. Bradley on January 16, 2025, and reported that her pain was 
unchanged.  (PX5)  The physical examination was unchanged.  (Id.)  Dr. Bradley reviewed read 
the MRI as showing a SLAP tear involving the biceps tendon, mild AC joint arthropathy and 
supraspinatus tendinopathy with no tear.  (Id.)  Dr. Bradley diagnosed a left SLAP tear and ordered 
physical therapy.  (Id.) 
On February 18, 2025, the Petitioner underwent a Section 12 examination by Dr. Timothy 
Farley, an orthopedic surgeon at MotionOrthopaedics.  (RX2)  As to the shoulder pain she 
experienced in May 2024, the Petitioner was not sure what led up to it and said she woke up with 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 4 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
discomfort.  (Id.)  She said that afterwards, she would try to avoid activities that would cause 
symptoms, such as weightlifting.  (Id.)  She described the November 12, 2024, accident 
consistently with her testimony.  (Id.)  Dr. Farley did not get the impression that she was 
exaggerating her complaints but said she came off as “somewhat standoffish.”  (Id.) 
Dr. Farley reviewed the medical records from after the work accident and examined the 
Petitioner.  (Id.)  He found significant tenderness at the AC joint and pain with cross-body 
adduction.  (Id.)  The Petitioner’s range of motion actively was slightly decreased on the left 
compared to the right, and passive range of motion was somewhat better with pain noted at the 
extremes of motion, which Dr. Farley said was possibly consistent with an underlying level of 
adhesive capsulitis.  (Id.)  Impingement, SLAP and biceps testing (Neer, Hawkin’s, O’Brien’s and 
Speeds) were positive.  (Id.)  Dr. Farley said the examination led to “reported results that are 
typically subjectively related to the patient’s response” and said any range of motion findings 
would simply be subjective guarding on the Petitioner’s part.  (Id.)  He reviewed reports from the 
two MRIs but not the scans themselves.  (Id.) 
Dr. Farley diagnosed left shoulder AC joint pain and possible low-grade adhesive 
capsulitis.  (Id.)  He did not think the Petitioner’s symptoms related to a rotator cuff tear, mainly 
because they rarely occur in 42-year-olds without some specific traumatic event – based on his 
decades of experience.  (Id.)  He thought the first MRI dictation probably overstated rotator cuff 
pathology, and the second likely represented a cleaner view of the state of the shoulder.  (Id.) 
Dr. Farley also did not think the Petitioner had a symptomatic labrum tear, as such tears 
that did not affect the biceps or biceps attachment “do not bother people.”  (Id.)  He said there is 
no mechanism for such tears to be symptomatic unless there is a large flap component, which was 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 5 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
not described in the radiology report.  (Id.)  He said there was no indication to consider any 
treatment of a non-displaced labrum tear that does not affect the biceps or biceps anchor.  (Id.) 
As to a causal connection between the Petitioner’s current condition and the accident, Dr. 
Farley said the Petitioner’s condition was pre-existing and under treatment.  (Id.)  He said she had 
“some degree of symptoms” leading up to the work accident that had never fully resolved.  (Id.)  
He thought the immediate evaluation and MRI were appropriate, but any subsequent treatment 
would be related to pre-existing issues.  (Id.)  He placed no restrictions on the Petitioner related to 
the work injury.  (Id.) 
The Petitioner underwent physical therapy at Athletico Physical therapy from January 22, 
2025, through February 24, 2025, for a total of 11 visits.  (PX7)  She testified that it “helped a little 
bit,” but the pain still continued.  (T. 17)  On February 27, 2025, she returned to Dr. Bradley and 
reported no change in her symptoms.  (PX5)  Dr. Bradley stated that the Petitioner’s range of 
motion and strength had improved, but she continued to have significant pain.  (Id.)  Impingement 
tests, SLAP testing and biceps testing were all positive.  (Id.)  He said her examination findings 
were consistent with a SLAP tear and recommended left shoulder arthroscopy with a biceps 
tenodesis and possible labral repair.  (Id.) 
The Petitioner underwent pre-operative testing on March 5, 2025, at SIU Medicine and 
SIH Memorial Hospital Carbondale and was cleared for surgery.  (PX8, PX9) 
Dr. Farley issued an addendum report on April 10, 2025, after reviewing the December 19, 
2024, MRI, which he identified as being from February 19, 2024.  (RX3)  He said he “really” did 
not see any evidence of a labrum tear, adding that the Petitioner had a slight meniscoid-type 
superior labrum, which he said was a normal variant.  (Id.)  His opinions did not change.  (Id.) 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 6 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
Dr. Farley testified consistently with his reports At a deposition on April 15, 2025.  (RX4)  
He stated that he prepared the addendum report after reviewing the MRI imaging, which did not 
change his opinions from the original report.  (Id.)  He said the MRIs showed the Petitioner had 
no rotator cuff tear.  (Id.)  Regarding the second MRI, he agreed with Dr. Schoen’s interpretation 
that there were insertional supraspinatus tendonitis and subinsertional infraspinatus changes but 
no high-grade partial-thickness or full-thickness rotator cuff tear.  (Id.)  He said that what was 
observed as a labral tear was a normal, meniscoid-type superior labrum because the cartilage goes 
over the bop of the socket, and the labrum never attaches to cartilage but attaches to bone.  (Id.)  
He said it will look like there is signal between the bone and the labrum but is not a tear but a 
normal variant.  (Id.)  He said both MRIs showed AC joint arthritis, and the Petitioner’s main area 
of pain was at her AC joint.  (Id.)  He thought “definitely” that the AC joint was leading to the 
Petitioner’s complaints.  (Id.)  During his testimony, Dr. Farley interchanged meniscus with 
labrum, but corrected himself.  (Id.) 
Although he said future treatment would not be related to the work accident, he said that if 
the Petitioner’s pain did not get better, he probably would consider an operation, specifically an 
examination under anesthesia and an open distal clavicle resection to address the AC joint pain.  
(Id.)  He said the labrum would not need repair because it and the biceps were healed to the bone 
with just fraying of the edges of the labrum.  (Id.) 
On cross-examination, he agreed that the Petitioner’s symptoms improved by avoiding 
weightlifting, but she stated they got worse after the work incident.  (Id.)  He acknowledged that 
he didn’t see anything in the records that the Petitioner’s symptoms after the accident returned to 
what they were before the accident.  (Id.)  He agreed that in reviewing OISI’s records, there was 
no “definitive” recommendation for surgery before the work accident.  (Id.) 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 7 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
Dr. Bradley testified consistently with his records at a deposition on May 9, 2025.  (PX10)  
He noted that prior to the work accident, the Petitioner didn’t have significant pain in her shoulder 
and was able to do all of her necessary job activities.  (Id.)  He said the Petitioner probably had 
some rotator cuff tendonitis and, maybe, a partial-thickness tear.  (Id.)  He did not appreciate a 
labral tear on the first MRI.  (Id.)  He said a labrum tear was “pretty clear” on the second MRI.  
(Id.)  He said the Petitioner’s AC joint degenerative changes were “very, very mild.”  (Id.) 
Dr. Bradley disagreed with Dr. Farley’s opinion that surgery was not indicated, adding that 
the Petitioner had been through nonoperative treatment, and her shoulder was “severely affected.”  
(Id.)  He said he didn’t understand why Dr. Farley said there was no biceps tendon involvement 
because tests performed during Dr. Farley’s physical examination were positive for biceps tendon 
and SLAP tears.  (Id.)   
As to the Petitioner’s AC joint, Dr. Bradley said his and Dr. Farley’s examinations differed 
in that Dr. Farley was able to elicit pain in the AC joint during a cross-body test, while his 
examination showed the majority of the Petitioner’s symptoms were coming from the biceps 
tendon.  (Id.)  He also did not know what Dr. Farley was referring to when he said the Petitioner 
had a meniscoid-type labrum because the meniscus is in the knee.  (Id.) 
The Petitioner testified that she wants the surgery so she can return to work and get back 
the mobility in her shoulder.  (T. 18)  She said it is painful to reach behind her back, lift anything 
above her head or lay on it.  (Id.)  She denied having those symptoms immediately before the 
accident.  (Id.)  She said that in May 2024, she did not have the burning sensation and could reach 
behind her back.  (T. 19)

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
 
The Arbitrator adopts the above Findings of Fact in support of the Conclusions of Law as 
set forth below. 
 
Issue (F):  
Is Petitioner’s current condition of ill-being causally related to the accident? 
 
An accident need not be the sole or primary cause as long as employment is a cause of a 
claimant’s condition.  Sisbro, Inc. v. Indus. Comm’n, 207 Ill. 2d 193, 205, 797 N.E.2d 665, 278 
Ill.Dec. 70 (2003).  An employer takes its employees as it finds them.  St. Elizabeth’s Hosp. v. 
Workers’ Comp. Comm’n, 371 Ill.App.3d 882, 888, 864 N.E.2d 266, 309 Ill.Dec. 400 (5th Dist. 
2007).  A claimant with a preexisting condition may recover where employment aggravates or 
accelerates that condition.  Caterpillar Tractor Co. v. Industrial Comm., 92 Ill. 2d 30, 36, 440 
N.E.2d 861, 65 Ill.Dec. 6 (1982).   
Circumstantial evidence, especially when entirely in favor of the Petitioner, is sufficient to 
prove a causal nexus between an accident and the resulting injury, such as a chain of events 
showing a claimant's ability to perform manual duties before accident but decreased ability to still 
perform immediately after accident. Pulliam Masonry v. Industrial. Comm'n, 77 Ill. 2d 469, 471-
472, 397 N.E.2d 834, 34 Ill.Dec. 162 (1979); Gano Elec. Contracting v. Industrial Comm'n, 260 
Ill.App.3d 92, 96–97,  631 N.E.2d 724, 197 Ill.Dec. 502 (4th Dist. 1994); International Harvester 
v. Industrial Com., 93 Ill.2d 59, 63-64, 442 N.E.2d 908, 66 Ill.Dec. 347 (1982). 
The Petitioner had issues with her left shoulder six months prior to the work accident and 
was supposed to undergo surgery.  However, the surgery that had been recommended was for the 
rotator cuff, while the injuries at issue here are to the SLAP and biceps tendon.  There is no 
indication that the Petitioner had injuries to her SLAP or biceps tendon prior to the accident.   
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 9 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
Dr. Farley diagnosed the Petitioner with left shoulder AC joint pain and possible low-grade 
adhesive capsulitis that he said were pre-existing conditions.  Dr. Bradley diagnosed a SLAP tear 
and found no issues with the AC joint other than mild arthritis. 
The Arbitrator notes issues with Dr. Farley’s opinions.  First, he rendered his opinions 
without having seen the MRI films.  Second, he did not reconcile his opinions with the Petitioner 
having positive examination tests for her SLAP and biceps tendon.  On the other hand, the bases 
for Dr. Bradley’s opinions were consistent with the physical examinations, as well as the 
radiologist’s reading of the second MRI.  In addition, as the treating physician, Dr. Bradley had 
more opportunities to become familiar with the Petitioner and her condition.  For these reasons, 
the Arbitrator gives more weight to Dr. Bradley’s opinions. 
Lastly, the Arbitrator finds that the circumstantial evidence supports a finding of causation.  
Although she had shoulder symptoms prior to the accident, she was able to perform her work duties 
and was willing to put off a proposed surgery for seven months.  After the work accident, her 
abilities were limited.  She testified that her symptoms were different after the accident and 
included burning pain, pain when reaching behind her back and inability to lift anything above her 
head or lay on her shoulder.  Dr. Farley acknowledged that the Petitioner’s complaints were worse 
after the accident, and she did not return to her pre-accident condition. 
Therefore, the Arbitrator finds that the Petitioner’s current left shoulder condition is 
causally related to the work accident. 
 
Issue (J): 
Were the medical services that were provided to Petitioner reasonable and 
necessary? Has Respondent paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary 
medical services? 
 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 10 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
The right to be compensated for medical costs associated with work-related injuries is at 
the very heart of the Workers' Compensation Act. Hagene v. Derek Polling Const., 388 Ill. App. 
3d 380, 383, 902 N.E.2d 1269, 1273 (2009). 
Dr. Farley did not find that the treatment thus far was unreasonable or not necessary.  His 
objection was to future treatment being causally related to the work accident.  Based on this and 
the findings above regarding causation, the Arbitrator finds the medical services provided were 
reasonable, and the Respondent has not paid the expenses for these services. 
Therefore, the Arbitrator orders the Respondent to pay the medical expenses contained in 
Petitioner’s Exhibit 1 pursuant to Section 8(a) of the Act and in accordance with medical fee 
schedules.  The Respondent shall have credit for any amounts already paid or paid through its 
group carrier.  Respondent shall indemnify and hold Petitioner harmless from any claims arising 
out of the expenses for which it claims credit.  
 
Issue (K): 
Is Petitioner entitled to any prospective medical care? 
 
Upon establishing causal connection and the reasonableness and the necessity of 
recommended medical treatment, employers are responsible for necessary prospective medical 
care required by their employees. Plantation Mfg. Co. v. Indus. Comm’n, 294 Ill.App.3d 705, 691 
N.E.2d. 13 (1997). This includes treatment required to diagnose, relieve, or cure the effects of 
claimant's injury.  F & B Mfg. Co. v. Indus. Comm'n, 325 Ill. App. 3d 527, 758 N.E.2d 18 (2001). 
An important function of the Act is to give workers the treatment necessary to try to return 
them to the conditions they were in prior to their work accidents.  Although efforts have been made 
to return the Petitioner to her pre-accident state, this has not been accomplished, and treatment 
options have not been exhausted.  Therefore, the Arbitrator finds that the Petitioner is entitled to 
26IWCC0141

BROWN, SARAH 
Page 11 of 11 
24 WC 33630 
 
prospective medical care, specifically surgery and follow-up treatment as recommended by Dr. 
Bradley.  The Respondent shall authorize and pay for such. 
 
In no instance shall this award be a bar to subsequent hearing and determination of an 
additional amount of medical benefits or compensation for a temporary or permanent disability, if 
any.
